# Starter: schedule-conflict catalog filter

This is a small, standalone TypeScript project (not part of the Berkeleytime
monorepo) modeling a real design problem from Berkeleytime's course catalog: a
filter criterion that depends on data the catalog's own paginated query
doesn't index.

## Setup

```bash
cd starter
npm install
npm test          # run the test suite once
npm run test:watch  # rerun on file changes
npm run typecheck   # tsc --noEmit
```

## The scenario

`src/catalog.ts` simulates a paginated catalog/search endpoint:
`getCatalogPage(pageNumber, pageSize)` returns a page of `CatalogSection`
fixtures (`src/fixtures.ts`), sorted and paginated the way a real backend
query would be. It has no idea any particular student's schedule exists.

`src/fixtures.ts` also exports `STUDENT_SCHEDULE`, a fixture schedule with
two already-enrolled sections. Several of the 40 catalog sections overlap
those sections' meeting times.

`src/scheduleFilter.ts` exports `getFilteredCatalogPage(pageNumber, pageSize,
studentSchedule)`, which is supposed to return only the catalog sections
that do **not** conflict with the student's schedule, correctly paginated:
every page except the true last page should have exactly `pageSize`
non-conflicting items, and `totalCount`/`totalPages` should describe the
non-conflicting catalog, not the raw one.

Right now, `getFilteredCatalogPage` is a stub -- it throws `not
implemented`. The JSDoc comment above it spells out the full contract it
needs to satisfy.

## The task

Implement `getFilteredCatalogPage` in `src/scheduleFilter.ts` so that every
test in `test/scheduleFilter.test.ts` passes, based on the design you worked
out in Round 1 (or a revised one, now that you can see the concrete types
and fixtures). Read the contract comment above the function and the
comments in `src/fixtures.ts` first -- they spell out the exact behavior the
tests check for.

Do not edit the test file or the fixtures. If you think a test is wrong, say
so in your writeup instead of changing it. You may implement
`getFilteredCatalogPage` however you like (call `getCatalogPage` more than
once per call, buffer state between calls, walk the whole raw catalog up
front, whatever) as long as its exported signature is unchanged.

This should take a competent engineer roughly 1-2 hours of the 3-4 hour
slot, including using whatever AI tools you'd normally use for this kind of
task. The remaining time is for the code review discussion.

## AI tool usage

Use AI tools however you normally would. Please keep a plain-text or
markdown log of the prompts you used (a running log is fine -- doesn't need
to be polished) and bring it to the code review. We're interested in how you
used the tool, what you kept vs. rejected, and where you double-checked its
output -- not whether you used one at all.
